sections.rule: One correct option. One mark each. No negative marking.
Multiple correct options. +1 for each right option, −1 for each wrong one, and a question cannot score below zero.

paper.caselet: A new privacy requirement invalidates a planned data feature, but the roadmap still shows it as committed.
paper.stem: What is the responsible product response?
options: Trace the affected requirement, revise priorities and the roadmap, and communicate how the strategic outcome will be met safely.
Hide the change from the stakeholders until after the release has already gone out to customers in production.
Build it unchanged, because a published roadmap cannot be moved once it has been committed to publicly.
Delete the privacy requirement from the backlog entirely so that the original delivery date can still be held as promised.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation?
options: MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: A numeric score eliminates the need to examine the assumptions that produced that number in the first place anyway.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: Every stakeholder request should be marked a Must have so that nobody involved is left disappointed.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: RICE ignores effort and confidence entirely, and ranks competing ideas on reach and impact alone when scoring them.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation: MoSCoW sorts necessity and RICE compares reach, impact, confidence and effort; neither ever replaces judgement.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Jobs to be done?
options: Jobs to be done: Jobs to be done always covers functional, emotional and social progress, never merely the product category or the stated feature.
Jobs to be done: A product category defines the same job for every single user, so one category description will cover everyone who sits in that whole market anyway.
Jobs to be done: Only the functional task matters, since confidence and social context are irrelevant to whether the customer's job gets done.
Jobs to be done: The job is the list of features that customers ask developers to copy from a competing product they happen to have already seen somewhere else.

paper.caselet: A patient asks for online consultation but mainly needs quick access to a trusted doctor and confidence that the advice is legitimate.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Jobs to be done: Design around access, trust and reassurance, because the named feature is never the whole job.
Jobs to be done: Ignore the emotional need entirely, because anything that is not functional cannot be part of the job.
Jobs to be done: Assume every telehealth user values exactly the same outcome from the consultation they have booked.
Jobs to be done: Optimise only the video resolution, because that is the feature the customer actually named.

paper.caselet: A student can state what TAM, SAM, and SOM is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects TAM, SAM, and SOM to the wider subject?
options: Once TAM, SAM, and SOM has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
TAM, SAM, and SOM works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Market sizing becomes actionable by narrowing theoretical need through service constraints to the customers the current product can actually win.
TAM, SAM, and SOM improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Competition and alternatives?
options: Competition and alternatives: Only firms shipping the same feature list should be counted as competitors in this particular market.
Competition and alternatives: Competition should be defined first, before anyone works out the customer's underlying job.
Competition and alternatives: Competition includes every current or potential way customers accomplish the job, including substitutes and doing nothing—not only similar products.
Competition and alternatives: Customers cannot compare a product against manual work or against doing nothing about the problem.

paper.caselet: A student can state what MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation to the wider subject?
options: MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once MoSCoW and RICE prioritisation has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Prioritisation turns scarce capacity into an explicit decision by separating necessity from comparative value and evidence.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Value-based pricing?
options: Value-based pricing: All customer segments receive the same value from the product and should therefore be charged an identical price for it.
Value-based pricing: Value-based pricing always starts from measurable customer value and willingness to pay, never from cost or the competitor's price.
Value-based pricing: Value can be priced without ever being articulated or measured, since the customer already knows what it is worth to them anyway.
Value-based pricing: Price should always equal unit cost plus a fixed markup, whatever the customer actually gains from using it.

paper.caselet: A new enterprise tool delights technical pioneers but mainstream buyers ask for uptime, integration, references, security, and support.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Crossing the chasm: Dismiss the reliability concerns as ordinary resistance to innovation coming from the more conservative buyers.
Crossing the chasm: Target the whole market at once, before proving that even one repeatable use case works reliably.
Crossing the chasm: Win a narrow beachhead with a complete, credible solution and use its references before expanding.
Crossing the chasm: Add more experimental features aimed at every possible segment at the same time.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Competition and alternatives is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Competition and alternatives to the wider subject?
options: The customer's job defines the competitive field; positioning improves when the product beats the real behaviour it must replace.
Competition and alternatives improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Competition and alternatives works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once Competition and alternatives has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Crossing the chasm is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Crossing the chasm to the wider subject?
options: Crossing the chasm works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Crossing the chasm improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Once Crossing the chasm has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Early enthusiasm proves possibility; mainstream adoption depends on reducing the practical and social risk of switching.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Crossing the chasm?
options: Crossing the chasm: Mainstream users tolerate more risk and missing support than early adopters do, since they arrive later and therefore expect a good deal less.
Crossing the chasm: The best strategy is to broaden to every segment at once, before building any references or support structure at all.
Crossing the chasm: Crossing to mainstream customers always requires a focused beachhead, a complete experience, references and lower adoption risk.
Crossing the chasm: Mainstream adoption follows automatically once innovators approve, because the early verdict carries across to the whole market.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Desirability, feasibility, viability?
options: Desirability, feasibility, viability: A product opportunity must be wanted by customers, technically achievable, and economically sustainable; strength in only two dimensions leaves a predictable failure.
Desirability, feasibility, viability: A feasible and profitable concept does not need demonstrated customer demand, because the economics on paper already justify the decision to build it.
Desirability, feasibility, viability: Desirability means that the team can actually engineer the product to the quality standard that the market has come to expect of it.
Desirability, feasibility, viability: Viability is proven whenever users say they like an idea, since stated enthusiasm eventually converts into paid revenue at scale over enough time.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Product definition and positioning is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Product definition and positioning to the wider subject?
options: Product definition and positioning improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Definition aligns builders on the solution; positioning helps a chosen customer understand why that solution matters and is different.
Once Product definition and positioning has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Product definition and positioning works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Functional and quality requirements?
options: Functional and quality requirements: Security and performance are always optional feature requests that can be added later on if there is time.
Functional and quality requirements: Quality requirements do not need measurable conditions attached to them, since their general intent is already understood by everyone on the team.
Functional and quality requirements: A functional requirement describes only the colour and layout of the user interface as it finally appears on the screen.
Functional and quality requirements: Functional requirements state what the product must do and quality requirements how well; a capability is never complete without both.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Requirements traceability?
options: Requirements traceability: Once a requirement is written down, its original source and its tests can safely be discarded from the record.
Requirements traceability: Traceability is only a list of developer tasks kept inside the team's project tracking tool.
Requirements traceability: Customer requirements and project requirements should never be connected to one another anywhere in the documentation.
Requirements traceability: Traceability links every customer need through requirement, implementation and verification, so scope and change stay explainable.

paper.caselet: A regulated Indian investing app could theoretically help global investors but can currently serve Indian online retail users and initially targets cost-conscious self-directed investors.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: TAM, SAM, and SOM: Treat global investors as TAM, Indian online retail investors as SAM, and the reachable cost-conscious segment as SOM.
TAM, SAM, and SOM: Call all global investors SOM, because a digital product can technically reach any one of them anywhere in the world.
TAM, SAM, and SOM: Call the initial segment TAM, because that is the group which will be contacted first in the campaign.
TAM, SAM, and SOM: Ignore regulation entirely when defining SAM, since rules do not change who could theoretically buy.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Functional and quality requirements is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Functional and quality requirements to the wider subject?
options: Once Functional and quality requirements has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Functional and quality requirements improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Functional and quality requirements works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
A capability is incomplete without the quality conditions that make it safe, usable, and compliant in the real product.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Unit economics is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Unit economics to the wider subject?
options: Unit economics improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Growth consumes cash before contribution repays acquisition; per-unit economics shows whether scaling improves or deepens the problem.
Unit economics works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Once Unit economics has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.

paper.caselet: A recommendation feature increases engagement but uses sensitive data outside the purpose users accepted.
paper.stem: Which decision best joins performance and responsibility?
options: Update the privacy notice on the site while continuing exactly the same processing underneath it as before the change was made.
Stop or redesign the data use, preserve purpose and consent, and measure whether a compliant alternative still delivers customer value.
Keep it running, because engagement is the highest product metric the team currently reports to the board.
Remove the engagement metric from the dashboard altogether so that the issue appears to disappear from view.

paper.caselet: A login system must authenticate users and block unauthorised access within a defined response time.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Functional and quality requirements: Treat authentication as functional, and security and response-time conditions as quality requirements that constrain its implementation.
Functional and quality requirements: Omit the security condition because a login screen already exists somewhere in the product today.
Functional and quality requirements: Record response time only after release, not as a requirement.
Functional and quality requirements: Treat every statement in the list as the same kind of feature label.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Lean Canvas is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Lean Canvas to the wider subject?
options: Once Lean Canvas has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Lean Canvas works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Lean Canvas improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system can be treated as somebody else's problem to solve later on.
A compact model makes linked business assumptions visible so learning can change the whole system rather than one feature at a time.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Privacy by design?
options: Privacy by design: All personal data may be reused for any new purpose whenever it improves a feature.
Privacy by design: Privacy by design makes lawful purpose, consent, minimisation, protection, user rights, and compliant partners part of the product from the start.
Privacy by design: Privacy is a notice added to the site once the data collection is already complete.
Privacy by design: A firm can ignore its partners' data practices entirely once the processing work has been outsourced to them.

paper.caselet: A team has a technically feasible product for a huge TAM but cannot name the customer progress it improves.
paper.stem: What should happen before scaling?
options: Set a price for the product before identifying what customer outcome it is actually meant to deliver for anyone who buys it.
Add more features to the product, because demonstrated technical feasibility is itself proof of real customer value here.
Return to the customer job and desirability evidence, then narrow to a reachable segment whose unmet progress the product can serve.
Increase the TAM estimates until the business case finally works on the spreadsheet in front of you.

paper.caselet: An early startup needs to decide whether a problem is worth solving and which assumptions an MVP should test.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Lean Canvas: Use Lean Canvas to expose problem, solution, metrics, advantage, segments, channels, costs, and revenue as testable assumptions.
Lean Canvas: Avoid revising the canvas once evidence arrives, since the original plan should be allowed to hold.
Lean Canvas: Fill only the solution box and treat the rest as execution detail.
Lean Canvas: Use it as a final audited financial statement for the board to sign off.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Unit economics?
options: Unit economics: A long payback period cannot create any cash-flow risk, as long as the lifetime value is high enough to cover it eventually.
Unit economics: Rapid revenue growth proves healthy unit economics automatically, because a fast-growing top line eventually covers everything underneath it in the end.
Unit economics: CAC should be compared with total revenue rather than gross contribution, because revenue is the number the customer actually pays each month.
Unit economics: Unit economics always tests profitability per customer or transaction: acquisition cost, contribution, lifetime value, churn and payback.

paper.caselet: Software saves one segment ₹10 lakh a year but saves another only ₹50,000, while serving both costs roughly the same.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Value-based pricing: Ignore the measurable savings the customer gains, because software has a low marginal cost.
Value-based pricing: Use the different economic value and willingness to pay to shape segment-specific offers and price structure.
Value-based pricing: Charge both segments from an identical delivery cost, since the software is the same.
Value-based pricing: Set the price from the cheaper alternative's feature count alone.

paper.caselet: A team publishes exact five-year feature dates although technology, regulation, and customer evidence are changing quickly.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Product roadmap: Freeze every feature date in place in order to protect the credibility of the originally published plan.
Product roadmap: Keep the direction and outcome sequence, but never present distant work at near-term detail.
Product roadmap: Remove the long-term direction altogether and keep only the tasks that the team happens to be working on right now.
Product roadmap: Treat the roadmap as a sales contract carrying no uncertainty at all for the customer who has signed it.

paper.caselet: A subscription spends ₹1,000 to acquire a customer and earns ₹100 monthly gross profit from that customer.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Unit economics: Recognise a ten-month CAC payback before considering retention, cash burn, and whether lifetime gross profit comfortably exceeds acquisition cost.
Unit economics: Compare CAC only with the top-line company revenue and stop the analysis there without looking at contribution.
Unit economics: Call the payback period one month, because the subscription happens to bill on a monthly cycle to the customer each time.
Unit economics: Ignore churn entirely, because the acquisition has already happened and that cost is already sunk anyway.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Requirements traceability is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Requirements traceability to the wider subject?
options: Traceability preserves the reason behind work, making change impact and completion evidence visible across the development chain.
Requirements traceability improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Requirements traceability works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Once Requirements traceability has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Actionable product metrics is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Actionable product metrics to the wider subject?
options: Once Actionable product metrics has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Actionable product metrics improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
A metric earns its place when evidence can change resource allocation, product action, or risk response.
Actionable product metrics works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Buyer journey communication is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Buyer journey communication to the wider subject?
options: Buyer journey communication works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once Buyer journey communication has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Buyer journey communication improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Customers need different information before they can take each next step; timing turns product value into understandable evidence.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Value-based pricing is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Value-based pricing to the wider subject?
options: Once Value-based pricing has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Value-based pricing improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Pricing captures part of created value; clear segmentation and value evidence connect customer benefit to business viability.
Value-based pricing works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.caselet: An app collects broad personal data for an undefined future use and sends it to an unreviewed analytics vendor.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Privacy by design: Collect everything available now and decide what the stated purpose for it will be at some later point.
Privacy by design: Limit collection to a stated purpose, establish the lawful basis and user controls, protect the data, and verify the vendor's compliance before transfer.
Privacy by design: Treat the act of outsourcing as a complete transfer of legal responsibility to the vendor who now holds and processes the data on its behalf.
Privacy by design: Rely only on a long terms-of-service page that is published after the collection has already happened on the site.

paper.caselet: Potential users do not yet recognise a health-monitoring problem, but the campaign opens with a detailed comparison of advanced settings.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Buyer journey communication: Use the same decision-stage proof on audiences who are not yet aware that the problem exists at all.
Buyer journey communication: Add more technical detail into the very first message the buyer ever receives.
Buyer journey communication: First make the problem and relevant value understandable, then introduce alternatives and proof as the buyer advances.
Buyer journey communication: Wait until after the purchase is complete before explaining any of the value to the customer.

paper.stem: Select every strategy the lecture gives for crossing the chasm.
options: Raise the price at launch so mainstream buyers read it as quality
Focus on a narrow beachhead market rather than spray and pray
Address the early market and the mainstream at the same time to build volume faster
Build trust through uptime, security, support, compliance, and social proof
Simplify onboarding and the interface for mainstream users

paper.stem: Select every box that appears on the Lean Canvas but not on the Business Model Canvas.
options: Channels
Customer segments
Problem
Unfair advantage
Solution

paper.stem: Select every statement that matches why the lecture says metrics matter more in a startup.
options: They exist to report performance to investors on a fixed reporting cycle
They exist to reduce uncertainty as far as it can be reduced
The fundamental difference from a mature company is the level of uncertainty
A startup should report performance first and take up risk management once the business matures
Top line, bottom line, and net promoter score assume a steadier state than an early product has

paper.stem: Select everything that counts as competition on the lecture's definition.
options: Manual alternatives such as spreadsheets, consultants, or internal tools
Rival products in the same category
Only the firms the startup has publicly named as competitors
An alternative counts only once the customer has formally evaluated it
The customer deciding to carry on doing nothing

paper.stem: Select every statement that matches how the lecture presents the three-way framework.
options: Viability is settled once a working prototype exists
Desirability is validated with design skills and empathy for the customer
Feasibility asks whether the product can be built with the technology available today
A product that is desirable and feasible but not viable is unsustainable
Feasibility is confirmed by customer interviews showing people want the product

paper.stem: Select every statement that is correct about the privacy regimes as the lecture presents them.
options: GDPR was enacted in May 2018 and became a model for Switzerland, Canada, and Australia
GDPR protects any personal data irrespective of its sensitivity
Data protection by design means the customer must request that their data be protected
US data protection is a single federal regime covering every category of data alike
US data protection leaves employee data outside its data protection regulations

paper.stem: Select every business type paired with the unit the lecture assigns it.
options: The unit is whichever one makes the economics look strongest to investors
Marketplace — one customer lifetime
SaaS — one customer or account
E-commerce — one order
Ride-sharing — one ride

paper.stem: Select every statement that matches the lecture's definition of a requirement.
options: It is any feature already present in the product
It describes a future capability, which is why requirements are elicited before anything is built
Requirements are classified by which team will end up building them
It is a wish or need for a future product capability, or a condition required by standards, contracts, or regulations
It is only a capability a customer has explicitly asked for

paper.stem: Select every statement that matches how the lecture treats cost-based pricing.
options: It is the fallback for when you do not know how the product will be deployed, or what it does to the customer's business
It prices your own inputs rather than the customer's outcome
It is the method to prefer once the product has a measurable economic value peg
Billing by engineer hours at $50 or $200 an hour is the familiar software-services case
It is what the lecture recommends for software products in particular

paper.caselet:
Zerodha is an online investment platform. In principle anyone, anywhere, who wants to buy exchange traded securities or mutual funds could use it.

In practice not everyone can. Cross-border investing carries its own regulatory framework, which leaves the platform serving online retail investors in India.

And not all of those are available either. Twenty to forty lakh of them already have a broker — Kotak Securities, ICICI Direct, HDFC Securities. What is genuinely open is the cost-conscious investor who would rather save the brokerage and do their own research.
paper.stem: Select every statement that sizes this market correctly.
options: Regulation on cross-border investing narrows SAM to online retail investors in India
SOM is the figure to quote as the market when raising funds
TAM is every retail investor who could use the product, worldwide
SOM narrows further because incumbent brokerages already serve those investors
TAM is calculated last, by scaling the achievable share back up

paper.caselet:
A ride-hailing product has three months before its first release, and everyone wants something in it — customers, investors, the sales team.

The team writes down what it could build. Booking a ride. Taking payment. GPS tracking. Driver ratings, so a rider can choose between two drivers. Multi-stop planning, so they can drop someone off on the way. In-car entertainment that follows whoever is driving.

Six candidates, one release, and MoSCoW to sort them: must have, should have, could have, won't have.
paper.stem: Select every capability that belongs in must have for this release.
options: Booking a ride
Driver ratings that help a customer choose between drivers
Payments
GPS
Multi-stop route planning

paper.stem: Select every statement that matches how the lecture uses MoSCoW.
options: Won't have is part of the method, and stating it is what makes scope control real
It works as a filtering criterion, closer to a triage than to a ranking
It ranks every item against every other to produce one ordered list
Moscow refers to the capital city, where the technique was first formalised

paper.stem: Select every statement that matches how the lecture separates definition from positioning.
options: Positioning is written first, and the product vision is derived from it afterwards
Product positioning is how the product impacts users, and why they should use it
Product definition is what the product does, and is largely internal — the team and its partners build against it
Definition and positioning are two names for the same customer-facing statement

paper.caselet:
WhatsApp started in 2009, into a market that already had Skype, Yahoo Messenger, ICQ and plenty more.

It launched on iPhone. Android followed around the middle of 2011 — and the team already knew that a large share of the people it wanted were on Android, in Asia.

The rest arrived on its own schedule: message history search around 2011, chat backup after 2012. The company was acquired in 2014 still without end-to-end encryption.
paper.stem: Select every statement that reads this release history the way the course does.
options: A roadmap is a smart sequence for developing, releasing, and evolving a solution
Launching on iPhone first shows the team did not know where its users were
The Android delay was a resourcing accident rather than a decision
A roadmap is a set of releases with no strategic horizon behind it
The team launched on iPhone knowing a big chunk of its potential users were on Android in Asia

paper.stem: A customer says the product must send a message, and must deliver it within 200 milliseconds. Select every statement that classifies this correctly.
options: Sending the message is a functional requirement — an action the product performs
The 200-millisecond bound is functional, because it describes what the product does
Both halves are non-functional, because the customer stated them in one sentence
The 200-millisecond bound is non-functional — a quality, confirmed by measurement under load

paper.stem: Select every metric paired with what the lecture says it measures.
options: Average revenue per user — revenue divided across the user base
Gross margin — profitability measured after all below-the-line costs
Customer lifetime value — what a customer is worth across the whole relationship, not one transaction
Net promoter score — the startup-appropriate replacement for reducing uncertainty

paper.stem: Select every statement that matches the lecture's account of a roadmap.
options: It fixes the next three to six months and deliberately goes no further
WhatsApp launched first on iPhone, with the Android version arriving around 2011
It translates product strategy into a series of releases on a time axis
It lists the features to build without ordering them, leaving sequence to the team

paper.stem: Select every statement that matches how the lecture traces a need into a requirement.
options: Project requirements are written by the customer and passed to engineering unchanged
Customer requirements arrive already standardised, because customers state system requirements
Customer requirements describe business needs and aspirations rather than system specifications
Project requirements break a product requirement down for a release across smaller teams
Standardising generalises one customer's stated need so more customers of that nature are served by one product

paper.caselet:
A doctor has just finished her residency. She walks into a hardware shop and asks for a drilling bit and a drilling machine.

Ask her what she is hanging, and it turns out to be photos — one photo, really: her MD certificate. Ask why it has to go up on the wall, and the answer moves again. Her patients see it. New ones especially, she says, want to know they are with a qualified doctor. Ten years of her life went into earning it, and she is proud of it.

What she is buying is a drill bit, a frame, and a hole in the wall.
paper.stem: Select every need this purchase actually serves.
options: Habitual — the purchase repeats often enough that no decision is taken
Financial — the drill costs less than hiring someone to do it
Functional — the certificate has to go onto the wall
Emotional — pride in more than a decade of study
Social — new patients gain confidence they are seeing a qualified doctor

paper.stem: Select every failure the lecture names when value is communicated badly.
options: Using the wrong channels to carry the message
Pricing the product below the nearest competitor
Communicating too late, after the decision has already been taken
Publishing the product vision before the product definition
